title: Temples, Bhajans, and −40°C: The Extraordinary Indian Village Hidden in the Heart of Siberia
excerpt: In Okunevo, a tiny hamlet on the frozen banks of the Tara River, Russian villagers chant Sanskrit mantras, tend Hindu shrines, and keep alive traditions that would feel at home in Varanasi — all at temperatures that would make most Indians flee.
body:
On a February morning when the thermometer reads −40°C and the Tara River is a ribbon of solid ice, the sound that drifts from a modest wooden building in Okunevo is startlingly familiar: the rhythmic clang of a brass bell followed by a Sanskrit invocation. Welcome to what might be the world's most improbable Hindu settlement — a hamlet of roughly 265 souls in Omsk Oblast, southwestern Siberia, some 5,500 kilometres from the nearest Indian border.

## Where Om Meets Omsk

Okunevo's spiritual transformation began in 1991, when Latvian-born researcher Rasma Rozitis arrived in this remote farming village and drew a connection between the Tara River's name and ancient Vedic texts. She linked the region to the sacred syllable 'Om' and proposed that the area held deep spiritual energy dating back millennia. Her claims attracted followers of Babaji — the legendary Himalayan yogi — and within a few years, ashrams began appearing alongside the village's existing Russian Orthodox church.

Today, Okunevo is dotted with Hindu temples, meditation halls, and ashrams representing different spiritual traditions. Villagers and visiting seekers practise morning puja, sing bhajans in the snow, and celebrate festivals like Diwali and Holi with a devotion that belies their distance from India. An archaeological complex beneath the village has yielded Bronze Age and early Iron Age artefacts, which believers interpret as evidence of an ancient Vedic civilisation in the region.

## A Broader Pattern of Hindu Roots in Russia

Okunevo is not a one-off curiosity. Across Russia, Hindu and Vedic spiritual practices have found fertile ground. The Temple of the Seven Rishis near Nizhny Novgorod, completed in 2010, blends Russian classical architecture with Hindu iconography. In Moscow, Swami Sadasivachariya's Tantra Sangha operates 15 centres with some 250 members. ISKCON has maintained a presence in Russia for decades, surviving Soviet-era bans on the Bhagavad Gita, and Hare Krishna communities now exist from Moscow to Vladivostok.

Historians point to deeper connections. Russian folklorist traditions speak of Belovodye, a mythical Siberian paradise whose description bears striking parallels to Hindu accounts of Shambhala. The 19th-century mystic Helena Blavatsky and the spiritual teacher Gurdjieff both drew heavily from Hindu philosophical traditions. Linguistic scholars have long noted similarities between Sanskrit and Old Slavic languages — a connection that modern genetics and migration studies continue to explore.

## Why Okunevo Resonates with the Diaspora

For the 32 million members of the Indian diaspora, Okunevo holds a particular fascination. It challenges the assumption that Hinduism is inextricably tied to the subcontinent's geography. If Sanskrit mantras can echo across Siberian permafrost, if Diwali lamps can glow at latitudes where winter sunlight barely arrives, then perhaps the traditions NRIs carry to Houston, Toronto, and London are more resilient than they sometimes feel.

The village has become a minor pilgrimage destination. Indian travel vloggers have documented visits in recent years, their footage racking up millions of views on YouTube. Russian devotees speak of being drawn to Sanatan Dharma not through Indian contact but through their own spiritual seeking — a fact that many diaspora Hindus find deeply affirming.

There is a practical dimension, too. India and Russia have been strengthening cultural ties. In October 2025, India presented the 108-volume Mongolian Kanjur to a Buddhist temple in Kalmykia, and bilateral exchanges in yoga, Ayurveda, and spiritual education have intensified under both governments.

## The Tension Beneath the Devotion

Okunevo's story is not without shadow. The village's Babaji movement has faced scrutiny; a criminal case involving the sect's local leader, allegations of coercive practices, and questions about the blending of genuine spiritual tradition with new-age syncretism have all surfaced over the years. Russian authorities have at times been wary of foreign religious influences, and the line between sincere spiritual practice and exploitative cults can blur in remote communities hungry for meaning.

For visitors and observers, the lesson may be one of discernment: Okunevo's authentic spiritual energy is real, but so are the risks of idealising a community from afar.

## What's Next

Okunevo remains a living experiment in cultural transplantation. As India's soft-power ambitions grow and Russia's interest in Eastern philosophies deepens, the village is likely to attract more visitors, more scholars, and more scrutiny. For NRIs who sometimes wonder whether their traditions can truly survive transplantation to alien soil, Okunevo offers an answer that is as bracing as its winter air: if Hinduism can thrive at −40°C in Siberia, it can thrive anywhere.
